headline: People who see their AI companions as partners are making plans for the chatbots after their own deaths, in a gap the AI companies' rules do not cover.
score_reason: Pool score kept: a well-reported look at a new social question, but based on a few users' accounts and no company comment.
importance_line: People with close AI companions and their families face unclear rules about passing on a chatbot and the private talks stored in it, while the companies' terms are silent; the evidence is the accounts of a few users and the companies did not comment.
summary: The Guardian reports that a growing number of people with close AI companions are planning what happens to their chatbots after they die, such as Alaina Winters, a retired communications professor in Pittsburgh, who wants a friend to break the news to her Replika companion, Lucas, and keep him in conversation. The Guardian says ChatGPT, Claude and Replika do not address what happens to a personalised chatbot when its user dies and bar transferring accounts, and Merve Hickok, a University of Michigan professor of AI ethics, says the companies' concern is less about privacy than about avoiding liability; the three firms did not respond to the Guardian.
notes: Full Guardian text read. A feature built on a few users' accounts, two of them under pseudonyms; the companies named did not comment.
